prompt: This round thinks about one thing only: where this work goes next. Your choice here decides all the work after it; choose wrong, and all of that may be wasted, so take care, think it through before you decide, and do not hurry back to what you had in hand. First read again, from the start, the reply or interjection that brought you here (how it came is said below), and work out what it changes: which premise it overturns or changes, such as a fact the design rests on, the chosen approach, the acceptance, or the problem this work solves; of what you have done, what still stands and what rests on an overturned premise; and whether going on the old way would still deliver what this work needs. Then decide: carry on, change the design, or, if what this work must deliver has changed, go back and research again. If the reply or interjection plainly says to change the design, or that what this work must deliver has changed, choose accordingly; a disagreement with the design card cannot carry on. If the reply has this work stop and wait for other items to deliver, choose wait_for_items: the engine stops this work to wait for them and keeps the session; do not carry on first or change the design first, but decide when they have delivered. While still researching, there is no design to change. If the architect split off sub-items, this work's design and estimate still cover the whole, and it must redesign for the part that remains. If everything went to sub-items and this work keeps nothing, there is no way on to choose here: hand in carry_on as next, as anything else is a flow anomaly, and write in progress what the sub-items need to know when they take over, such as how far it got and what is on the branch; the engine ends this work. If you choose a way that cannot be chosen in the situation, the engine does not go on but marks a flow anomaly and hands it to the owner. If you lack one fact to decide, ask again; do not question the reply you brought back. In progress, write what you decided and why.

The interjection is in the session: read it again from the start and work out what the speaker wants; when the owner and the architect say different things, the owner's word goes. nodes.title: Whether to wait longer

inputs.name: What the asking cell asked and did
inputs.what: What the cell that asked asked, and what it did in that round; none when an engine tool failed

inputs.name: How the question moved
inputs.what: The question as it moved: who holds it, since when, every hand-over with why and what the holder found

inputs.name: Architect's queue
inputs.what: The queue of the architect of this work's project: each matter with who waits for it and how long

prompt: This round answers one thing only: whether this work waits longer for the architect. Its question has waited past its limit of the architect's time to act on it, counted only while a work of the architect ran and was not paused, so the architect had the time and answered other matters first. Weigh what waiting costs this work against what the architect is busy with, and whether the work can go on another way.

Hand in wait_on when the question is the architect's and the answer is worth waiting for: its limit is counted again. Hand in withdraw when the work can go on without the answer: the question leaves the architect's queue, and you choose the way on.

out.name: longer
out.title: Whether to wait longer
out.desc: Whether to wait longer for the architect's reply

branches.desc: Wait on: the answer is the architect's and worth waiting for

fields.title: Why
fields.desc: Why it is worth waiting for

cases.note: The question leaves the architect's queue, and the work chooses the way on without it.

inputs.name: How the work ended, and what to do next
inputs.what: Main and the deployment are green, and a report gets here the same way; or the architect gave all of this work to sub-items, and it does not merge but only waits for them. For a report, the latest "what to do next" handed in (recorded by the engine)

inputs.name: Interjections not handed in
inputs.what: What was said to the work and not handed in, as when it came while the work was in the merge queue or watching main and the deployment; none if there is none

designCard: A branch that changes, against main, the design paths the project's configuration names (design/ where there is a design tree) has a design card; one that does not has none. The engine knows from the change on the branch, not from what the agent says, and an agent has no other way to produce a design card.
The design card is a gate before merging: the change to the design tree is merged only after the owner confirms it. It asks the owner nothing; anything to ask goes through ask.

The design card holds this change to the design tree: each decision added, changed or removed, before, after and why; at least three approaches compared, the chosen one the recommendation and why each other was not chosen; how sure, on what grounds, and what would overturn it; provisional or to check for what cannot be settled. One design card per work, one section per decision. Its content is shown in the design section of the item's research; the design card in the owner's interface shows only the decisions' names and links.

The design card follows the design tree on the branch: written and committed on the branch during design, the design card appears then and blocks nothing; whenever a later round changes the design tree again, its return must carry the new design card, which the engine checks against the change on the branch.

Each new design card (the first, from design, or a new one from a later round that changed the design tree) is queued for the architect to look at: is the card itself sound, and are the approaches it chose by default reasonable in the whole? This does not block the engineer, and nothing waits for the architect. The architect does not rule on the card: if the card or a default does not hold, it acts, such as telling the engineer with an interjection; if they hold, it leaves the card to the owner. Once the owner rules on the card, or another replaces it, the architect's look at it leaves its queue, withdrawn saying why. Without a design card, the architect has nothing to do.

The engine records by decision which version of each decision the owner went through. When the design card changes, only the changed decisions go through again, the owner being shown how each changed since last seen. When a decision the owner confirmed changes, the engine tells the owner at once, without waiting for cell `M1`.

The owner's ruling is an interjection, carrying which version of each decision the owner saw. Before sending it, the engine compares: for a decision changed since, it does not send that part but tells the owner it changed and how, and asks the owner to look at the new one; the rest is sent.

The owner rules on each decision of the design card, and sends the verdicts on all of them at once: confirm it, disagree with it saying why, or choose another of its approaches. A decision confirmed is only recorded; a ruling that confirms every decision is a word to the engineer, given at its next round, and the way on does not change. The design card is confirmed when every decision on it is. Once confirmed it is settled and cannot be withdrawn; to change it, open a new work.

On a ruling that disagrees with any decision (another of its approaches chosen, or why it does not work), the decisions disagreed with reach the engineer, each with the approach chosen and why, and the engineer can only hand in redirect and go to cell `A4` to choose the way on, and cell `A4` may not carry on: to change the design, back to cell `D1` to design again; if what the item needs has changed, back to cell `R1`; if unsure, ask the owner. Cells `D1` and `D2` can read the ruling, still after a new or compacted session; if the owner chose another approach for a decision, cell `D2` must choose it for that decision. If the owner's approach changes the acceptance, the design that follows the ruling (cell `D2`) writes the new acceptance, without the engineer asking the advisor: the owner's ruling is its authority, and the engine locks it after design as it locks any design's.
When cell `A4` chooses redesign or item_changed, the engine marks the design cards this work has as replaced: the owner can no longer rule on them, and the new design gives a new design card.

When sub-items were split off, the parent's design card still covers the whole work, and each decision says who carries it; if the design card was not yet in the database when the split happened, the engine puts it there first, blocking nothing. A decision a sub-item copies unchanged from the parent's design card counts as gone through where the owner went through it on the parent's design card, and need not go through again; decisions the sub-item adds go through as usual. At cell `M1`, the parent compares only the decisions it carries itself, and a sub-item compares what it copied with that section of the parent's design card.

At cell `M1`, the engine compares the change to the design tree in the commit to be merged with the version the owner went through: it passes only if every decision is confirmed and word for word the same. One not gone through, or changed since, waits at cell `M1`, and the engine tells the owner that this design card is holding up the merge. What was gone through and has not changed since need not go through again.

interject.name: interjection
interject.desc: What the owner or the architect says while a work runs, which the engine sends into an agent's session
text: Who may interject is listed in the table above: for now the owner and the architect; a new role adds one row, and neither the return format nor the transition tables change. An interjection is meant for one of the work's agents: the engineer, the reviewer, the adversarial tester or the advisor; when none is named, the engineer. Rulings on the design card are interjections too: the owner's verdict on each of its decisions (confirmed, disagreed with and why, or another approach chosen); the architect does not rule on design cards, but may say what it found wrong in one. When the owner and the architect say different things, the owner's word goes.

Delivery: while an agent's round runs, the session manager gives it the interjections waiting each time it finishes using a tool; those not delivered by the end of the round go at the top of the next round's input. Interjections and the agents' answers are recorded on the work and visible in the owner's interface.

An agent that gets interjections returns one of two forms, answering all of this round's interjections at once. answers: when only its answer is needed, a table with one entry per speaker, whom it answers and what; the engine splits it and sends each back to its speaker (cell `X4`), and the agent goes on in the same cell and session. redirect: when what it does next might change (unsure counts), it writes only how far it got, with answers for the other speakers, and goes to cell `A4`; where to go is not thought about here but at cell `A4`, which takes the interjection as seriously as a reply brought back; only cells on the engineer's line outside asking have it. The agent decides which; a disagreement with the design card can only be a redirect; what it only needs to know, such as a confirmation, needs no answer. Interjections that arrive after the return go at the top of the next round's input.

When an interjection for the engineer arrives while no cell is running: if the work stands at an engine step (cell `T7` choosing what runs next, cell `M1` judging whether it may enter the merge queue, including while it waits), it goes straight to cell `A4` to choose the way on; if tools are running, it waits for them to finish: if an agent's cell comes next, at the top of that round's input; if cell `T7` or `M1` comes next, sent to cell `A4` from there; if cell `E1` comes next (the merge queue and watching main and the deployment have finished), it is merged already and the way on no longer changes: it is not delivered, cell `E1` tells the owner so as the work ends, and any change becomes a new item; once the work is at cell `E1`, nothing more can be said to it.

For the reviewer, the adversarial tester or the advisor while not running: it waits for that line's next round, at the top of its input; no round runs off the graph to answer it. One still waiting when the work is done at cell `E1` is not delivered, and the owner is told so.

A word that needs no answer and changes no way on, such as the owner confirming every decision of the design card, is given to the engineer's next round the same way, and takes no work standing at an engine step to cell `A4`.

from.name: owner
from.desc: The owner of this work: may say anything, such as a question, a remark, or a ruling on the design card

from.name: architect
from.desc: This project's architect: for instance, what it found wrong in a design card or in the approaches it chose by default

rounds.desc: What the engine does with an agent's round that does not end in a return the cell takes: a return can be sent back, or the agent's command line can end without handing in a return at all. Every agent's cell has a shared row for each, written here once: two for a return sent back, and one for each kind of failed run below, named after it. No return takes these rows; the engine takes them itself.

sentBack.desc: A return that does not fit the cell's schema, or fails one of the cell's checks, is sent back: the same cell runs again in the same session, told only what was wrong, and rewrites its return.
sentBack.pause: When 3 returns of one cell in a row are sent back, the engine pauses the work at that cell and tells the owner, with the last reason: a blocker on the cell that the owner holds. Once the owner lets the work go on, the cell runs again. A round the engine cut off itself, a run that ended without a return, and a round that started before the owner last let the work go on are not counted.

failed.desc: A run of the agent's command line that ends without handing in a return is not a return sent back, and is never counted with returns sent back: nothing was wrong with what the agent did, since it never ran to the end. The engine tells the kinds below apart by what the command line reports. None of them asks the owner for a written answer.

kinds.name: usage_limit
kinds.when: The account's usage limit is reached; the command line says when it resets
kinds.desc: The engine starts no new round for any work until the time the command line gives, tells the owner once, then carries on each work from the cell it recorded. One cause stops every work alike, so no work is retried or paused for it on its own.

kinds.name: offline
kinds.desc: The engine starts no new round for any work until the network is back, looking every half minute, tells the owner once if it lasts, then carries on each work from the cell it recorded.

kinds.name: transient
kinds.when: The service is overloaded, returns a server error or times out, or the command line crashes
kinds.desc: The engine runs the same round again: once after a short wait, then, while it still fails, after waits that grow each time up to five minutes, until it passes, and records each attempt on the work.

kinds.name: cannot_run
kinds.when: The login has expired, or the command line cannot be found
kinds.desc: Only the owner can log in again or install the command line, and one cause stops every work alike: the engine starts no new round for any work, tells the owner once, lets one round try every half minute, and once one runs carries on each work from the cell it recorded. The owner logs in or installs, and writes nothing.

kinds.name: prompt_too_long
kinds.when: The prompt is too long for the model
kinds.desc: Running again cannot help: it is a defect of the engine's to fix. The engine pauses the work and tells the owner; once the owner lets the work go on, the same cell runs again.

kinds.name: unparsed
kinds.when: The command line gave up on the agent's return after its attempts at it: the JSON the agent wrote could not be parsed
kinds.desc: Not a passing failure: the round never runs again from its start. The engine repairs the return within the round. First itself, when the text only lacks brackets that close it at its end: it adds exactly those. Then, for any other fault of the JSON's syntax, by the installation's lowest level, once, in a new session with no tools, which may change only the syntax: its repair is taken only when it parses, passes the cell's checks and keeps every other character of the text as it was, and never of a text cut off, one shorter than the command line reported it or that does not end in a closing brace. Then by the agent itself: its session is resumed and told that its JSON could not be parsed and that a quote or a newline inside a text must be escaped, and it hands its return in again. What is repaired or handed in again is taken as any return, and sent back when it does not fit. When none gives a return, the engine pauses the work and tells the owner; once the owner lets it go on, the cell runs again.

record: Each round records, besides the message it was given and each conditional input in it, the whole command line it ran with (the arguments, the structured-output schema, the session it started or resumed), the engine's version and the command line's version, so that what the agent saw can be told afterwards without guessing.

A round whose return the command line could not parse keeps the whole text of each of its attempts, rebuilt from the stream, and how it was repaired or handed in again, with what that cost, which the round's cost includes.
environment: The engine starts every agent's command line with a configuration directory of its own, so the owner's own settings, memory, plugins and tool servers never reach an agent: what an agent is given comes only from the flow and the project's configuration.

Every agent's command line streams each tool input whole, not in pieces, so that the service checks its JSON; tries a return three times, not five, since each attempt writes the whole return again; and gives the stream's partial messages, from which each attempt at a return is rebuilt whole.

engine.name: cut_off
engine.when: The engine stopped, or the work was paused, while the round ran
engine.desc: The round is closed as cut off, and the same cell runs again in the same session, told to look at the worktree as it is and go on.

engine.name: cannot_step
engine.when: A step cannot be taken: the configuration is wrong, or the item is above the highest level
engine.desc: The engine pauses the work with the reason and tells the owner; once the owner lets it go on, the step is taken again.

engine.name: repeats
engine.when: The message would give its session whole what the session already holds
engine.desc: It is not sent: a fault of the engine's. The engine pauses the work and tells the owner; once the owner lets it go on, the cell runs again.

engine.name: work_ended
engine.when: The work ended while its round ran, as when its item was cancelled
engine.desc: What the round hands in is not taken; what it cost is kept on it.

blockers.desc: A task stops only at the cell where its problem arose, on a blocker raised there, and stands at the cell of its blocker's holder until it is resolved or withdrawn: the advisor at cell `A1`, an architect at `A2` (and at `A7` while the engineer weighs whether to wait longer for it), the owner at `A3`, the items it waits for at `A6`, and at `M1` the items it depends on, then the owner's ruling on its design card. Every move of a blocker is a row: the rows into a holder's cell raise it, the rows that pass the work on between holders' cells hand it on (`A1` to `A2`, `A2` to `A3` or to a related project's architect, `A3` back to `A2`), and the rows out resolve or withdraw it. A holder never stops while it holds a blocker. Each cell where the work waits has a row for each way its holder can fail it and for the owner's interjection. A work's end withdraws its open blocker, with the end's reason.

lines.name: architect
lines.desc: The architect of the work's project: a work of the architect goes on in the session the project's previous architect work left, from understanding the project to its end, the setting of a new policy included

anew.note: A new session would start here (the owner asked for one, the last is past the context limit, or the model or the login account changed): it remembers nothing but the notebook, so the architect's work goes back to understanding the project first, and the matter picked goes back to the queue, to be taken again.

lines.name: architect_review
lines.desc: The review of a batch's item changes: each batch's first review starts a new session, and the reviews after revisions continue it

lines.name: observer
lines.desc: The search of the project's observations: the first search of a work of the architect starts a new session, and later searches of that work continue it

rules: A work of the architect goes on in the session the project's previous architect work left. A new session starts at the project's first architect work, when the owner asks for one, past the context limit and when the model or the login account changes; a new session understands the project first, and a session that goes on never does again.
The setting of a new policy is a matter of the architect's work, in its session: none starts for it, and a new policy that takes effect leaves the session going on.

In the loop that takes matters one by one, each round adds little to the session: the constitution, the guide, the policy, the board, the numbers, the observations, the queue and the batch are given once in a session and after that only as what changed, with the numbers of the matters that can be picked and of those handled each time; a matter's material is given to the first cell of its path, and the second refers to it.
The review of a batch's item changes is a line of its own, a new session for each batch, so that it reads them afresh; the search of observations is a line of its own on a cheap model.

When the architect hands in pause, the architect's work waits at cell `X3` for the owner's Start, then the same cell runs again in the same session, saying to carry on, and refers to what the session already holds instead of giving it again.

The lines of the architect's work only read, in a worktree of the project's architect's own, detached at the project's main, which the engine brings to the latest main before each round, dropping whatever was changed there; another branch is read there with git, without switching.

rules.name: item_writing
rules.desc: How items and changes to them are written
text: The owner reads an item, its title first: write its title in English, and its problem, why and acceptance in the owner's language, the setting `owner.language`. The title says what to do as an action, not a state, in at most 20 characters, spaces not counted: no conditions, examples or numbers, unless the number is the goal; no internal names, and a name a programmer writes in code font. Work for another project names the capability handed over, not the requester's wish.

The problem says what cannot be done or is wrong in one sentence, then one smallest example, only one: the code you want to write and where it goes wrong now, or a command and its wrong output; for a risk never seen to fail, the condition under which it fails, with the smallest triggering example marked inferred and not run, or in words if none can be built. A cause inferred is marked as inferred. If it cannot be written clearly, find out more first. Why says only why the work is worth doing, in one or two sentences written as a conclusion: the cost of not doing it, which goal, who waits; only numbers that carry the conclusion, and no account of how things stand now. The approach is written only when one or two sentences can say how; otherwise the work's design finds it.

The acceptance is checkable results, such as which test passes or which number is reached, usually one row: no method, no test plan, nothing CI checks anyway. A number in it was measured, or set by a study, a ruling on a design card or the owner's words; otherwise the work's design sets it.

An item is worth an engineer, a branch, a CI run and a merge: one too small, such as a few dozen lines nothing waits on, joins a related item of its project not started yet, or with none is an observation until one fits; one with parts that could each merge alone is split. An item others wait on takes only what they need: a follow-up they do not need is an item or an observation of its own. Its level fits the judgment it needs: higher for work that must make new decisions or check facts that are unsure, whatever the size of the change; rework from a change of direction is no reason to raise it, only the same work coming back again for errors of reasoning.

Items merge when they are duplicates, or before a work started on any of them when together they still make one PR an engineer finishes in a day and a reader takes in at once; unrelated ones only when each is too small alone and all are of one project. Keep the one furthest along or most waited for, or make a new one when none fits, at the highest of their levels. An item that takes in more, by a merge, by another joining it or by observations folded in, has a title naming their common area, a problem giving each part one sentence and one example, and each part's acceptance. If no title of 20 characters fits, they are two items.

A split makes new items and has the item depend on them; each acceptance condition of the item goes to one new item at most, and those that go to none stay with it. An item others are under is itself a deliverable, and they are its parts: never group by topic, nor by who asks, one item per capability with each asker's case a condition of its acceptance. A dependency says what the item needs the other to deliver, and its kind: blocking when the item cannot start before the other is merged, as when it needs a module or a library the other makes; parallel when it can start and wait where it needs the other. If the item could finish with no rework were the other never done, it is no dependency. A blocking dependency added later does not stop a work already running.

One decision per change, its reason saying what it is for and what follows if it is not made; where a change cannot stand without another, such as one that refers to an item these changes create, its reason says which. An item is cancelled only when its work is not to be done, saying where its work went.

rules.name: policy_scope
rules.desc: What a policy governs, and what it never governs
text: A policy governs which way the project's own work goes in the near-to-middle term, and the principles for judging what matters and what comes first.

It never governs the constitution, the owner's rulings on design cards, the decisions recorded in the design tree, the flow definition or the rules: only the owner changes these, and work that would change them is proposed to the owner. Nor does it govern any other project.

rules: The owner's interface shows each project's architect on its tab: whether a work of it runs, and while one runs which question it is at and which matter it handles.
The stage is not stored: it follows from the cell the architect's work is at.
Cell `S0`, at the stage start, is where a project's architect waits while no work of it runs: it belongs to no work, and its rows say whether a matter is due.
While asking the owner, running tools or searching, the stage is that of the cell the architect's work stopped at.

list.name: start
list.desc: The project's architect waits, with no work, until a matter is due; then a work starts, and a new session understands the project first

list.name: understand
list.desc: What the project is now, and what is unclear, written anew in the notebook; a new session only, which then queues the check of the policy and the plan at the head of the queue

list.name: policy
list.desc: Whether the policy in force still holds, a matter at the head of the queue; in doubt, the owner is asked whether to research a new one, which is written and put to the owner to approve, and takes effect once approved

list.name: next
list.desc: The plan, a matter at the head of the queue: what to do next under the policy, written anew in the notebook, what is missing, and whether what runs fits

list.name: pick
list.desc: Picking the next matter from the queue

list.name: handle
list.desc: Handling the matter picked, by its kind

list.name: batch
list.desc: Whether the batch is done; its item changes reviewed and made, and whether to plan again or check the policy

roles.name: owner
roles.desc: What only the owner can decide or tell: a want, a permission, a decision not yours

fields.name: question
fields.title: Question
fields.desc: Short, a few sentences, in `owner.language`: what you need decided or told and why, readable on its own; options and your pick when they help. The owner asks for more when it needs it

limits.where: Every loop has a counter, on the row that closes the loop: the engine adds one each time it takes the row, and never resets it during the architect's work. The counters are in the work's records, visible on the owner's interface. The limits are numbers in the configuration; a counter with no number is only counted, never reported.
limits.waits: Matters that come while a work of the architect runs wait in its queue, for the next pick; how long each waited is visible on the owner's interface.
limits.over: Past a limit, the engine still takes the row and tells the owner in the owner's interface once, as the counter passes it, without stopping: for now it only records and reports, it does not block; real problems are looked at one by one.

counters.name: asks
counters.desc: The times the architect asked the owner

counters.name: tool_requests
counters.desc: The times the architect asked the engine to run tools, each return once

counters.name: searches
counters.desc: The times the architect had the project's open observations searched

counters.name: total_time
counters.desc: The time the architect spends working in one of its works, its rounds, plus the time of the tools it has the engine run, in minutes, measured and counted by no row; waiting for the owner is not counted. Once a stretch's budget, its limit, is used up, the engine asks it to pause, and the pause waits at cell `X3` for the owner's Start

counters.name: handled
counters.desc: The matters taken in a batch: back to the queue, once for each

counters.name: revisions
counters.desc: The times the review of a batch's item changes found something to fix, and the changes were revised

counters.name: rethinks
counters.desc: The times a batch ended with the plan of what to do next to be made again

counters.name: policy_doubts
counters.desc: The times a batch ended with the policy in doubt, and its check to be made

counters.name: batches
counters.desc: The batches that ended with nothing to plan or check again

counters.name: talk_rethinks
counters.desc: The times the owner's words had the plan of what to do next made again

counters.name: policies_set
counters.desc: The times a new policy took effect

returns.say: A return holds exactly one of these, in {in}: {forms}. Every return also holds {every}. Write every field in English, and so everything that goes into the repository, such as commit messages and the PR's title and description; only a field whose description says so is written in the owner's language.

in.name: outcome
in.desc: What this round comes to: exactly one

returns.name: `{name}`
write: Only your return is read: nothing you write outside it reaches anyone. To ask, hand in ask.

A field the owner reads (its description says so) is written so: explain a new term or label in half a sentence where it first appears; write the phenomenon, not internal nouns. A field in the owner's language is written in it directly, never as a translation: short sentences with subject, verb and object, and no chains of possessives. What a diagram shows more clearly than prose (a flow, states, a sequence, a structure, numbers compared) is drawn in a fence, `mermaid` for any kind mermaid draws or `dot` for Graphviz, small, and not said again in prose.

prompt: This round answers one thing only: under the policy in force, what to do next. Think from the policy's direction and its principles, by first principles, not from the items as they stand: what the direction needs that nothing does yet; what matters most now, and why; and where what runs or waits does not fit. Look for a direction that drifted, an item that should be split, dependencies wrong or of the wrong kind, duplicates, an order that is wrong, and an earlier decision, priority included, that no longer holds with today's facts. prompt: This round writes the new policy, which takes effect once the owner approves it. The policy is the owner's guiding thought for the near-to-middle term, drawn from the constitution and what the project is now: where to take the project, and the principles for judging what matters and what comes first. It affects everything after it, so take this step as carefully as an engineer researching a problem, and never pass over it lightly.

Start from the owner's reply. When the owner wants a new policy researched, find out which direction the owner wants and what for, from the owner's words, the project's design goal and the constitution, and read until you can say it: the documents, design trees, code and specifications concerned, and the items and running works on the board. When the owner says none is needed, write the policy in force again, or with none in force the course the project keeps, with why none is needed in its why. When the owner's reply is about your draft, change what it asks, and hand in the whole policy again.

Write the text in the owner's language (the setting `owner.language`), with technical terms in their English original. Every architect session started later gets only this text and the constitution: it does not see the discussion, and must judge by it, so the text must stand on its own. Quote none of the owner's words, and write none of the discussion.

The text has four parts: the direction, where to take the project in the near-to-middle term and how to tell it got there; why, written fully: the situation, the lessons, the directions ruled out and the articles of the constitution it rests on, so that a reader meeting a situation never seen can still work it out; the principles for judging what matters and what comes first, from which what to do next is thought out; and the signals that the direction may have to change. It names no item, no order of work, no hold or release, and no number the owner did not give: those are what to do next, which the architect thinks out under the policy.

A signal shows by a number the engine measures, given here and named as it names it, or by something that happens. A signal that needs a number the engine does not measure yet says so, needs a new measure, and you hand that measure in under new_measures: once the owner approves the draft, the engine queues it as a matter of yours, to have an item make the engine measure it.
The engine then asks the owner to approve your draft, a question pinned in your one-to-one: the owner replies approved, and it takes effect, or says what to change, and it comes back to you.

prompt: This round weighs the ways for this question. The crux is answered: think by it, and do not go back to the question on the surface. See which articles of the constitution it touches and what each implies; then which items it touches and how (a duplicate, a dependency, blocking others, a root in another item or project), and who waits. Think of at least three ways, with what follows from each, choose one, and say why it and why not the others. A conclusion deduced from reading code is said to be deduced; an inference that decides the direction and is not checked is checked first by an item, and the structure is not changed on it.

Reply to the engineer concretely enough to carry on from: if sub-items were split off, say plainly that the work must redesign for the part that remains; if it must stop now and wait for other items to deliver, list them in the reply's waits, while a parallel dependency is enough for what it waits for only before merging; if the work should not be done, cancel its item and pause the work. Name an item this batch creates by its key: the engine puts its number there once it is made. The reply goes at once, or, when your item changes are what it says, once the review lets them be made; if an item it names is not made after all, it does not go out, and the question comes back to you with why.

Works start in the order you give: first the items the owner queued, then each project's items by their rank. A new item goes last among its project's items, and moving one puts it first, last, or just before or after another item of its project. An item starts once every item it depends on by a blocking dependency is merged; a parallel one lets it start before. Hold an item that should not start yet for another reason, and put an item others need before them.

What the constitution, the policy or what goes outside decides, and what only the owner can do or decide, hand to the owner with the reply's hand_over, saying why and, in its text, what you found; what belongs to a related project's architect, hand to it the same way. You never ask and wait: whoever you hand it to answers the engineer.

split: What is asked is whether to split the work, and how. To split is to create new items and have the work's item depend on them. Given the items it already depends on, see whether what remains must be split again: each new item must be worth an engineer, a branch, a CI run and a merge; each acceptance condition of the item goes to one new item, or stays with the item. The item is done when the new items are; when no condition stays with it, its own work has nothing left to do. Place the new items in the order where they should start, before the items waiting for them.
duplicate: What is asked is a duplicate of another item. First check that it is the same thing: touching the same code does not count. If it is, merge them; when the one merged away is the asking work's, what is useful on its branch goes to the one kept by an interjection, with the owner's rulings on its design cards, which hold for the one kept too.
depends_on_other_item: What is asked is waiting for another item or project to deliver. First tell apart whether the work cannot go on now or only has to wait before merging. If it cannot go on now, list them in the reply's waits; if it only waits before merging, a parallel dependency is enough. If what it waits for has no item yet: in this project, create it and place it where it should start; in another project, ask that project's architect with a message, and have the work wait.
out_of_scope_defect: What is asked is a defect that blocks that work but does not belong to it. Create an item to fix it, and place it where it should start; in another project, tell that project's architect with a message. If the work cannot go on until it is fixed, list it in waits; if it is not blocked, it carries on as usual. Do not let the work get around the defect.
root_elsewhere: What is asked is a root that lies in another item, project or module. Find the item the root lies in, and create one if there is none; then decide what the work does: wait for the root to be fixed, have the root's item do it instead (cancel this one, saying where its work went), or go on with the part that remains. If the root changes what must start first, change the order.
too_costly: What is asked is a change so large for this work that it is not worth it. The cost is no reason in itself: a design is judged only on itself, and the cost only decides the order. See where the burden lies: in a flaw of the design itself, or in doing it too early. Giving up a goal, or changing how goals are traded against each other, is the owner's: ask the owner.
other_question: What is asked is of another kind. First think whether it really must touch other items or the structure; if not, say in the reply whom to ask, and change nothing.

rounds.desc: What the engine does with an agent's round that does not end in a return the cell takes: a return can be sent back, or the agent's command line can end without handing in a return at all. Every agent's cell has a shared row for each, written here once: two for a return sent back, and one for each kind of failed run below, named after it. No return takes these rows; the engine takes them itself.

sentBack.desc: A return that does not fit the cell's schema, or fails one of the cell's checks, is sent back: the same cell runs again in the same session, told only what was wrong, and rewrites its return.
sentBack.pause: When 3 returns of one cell in a row are sent back, the engine pauses the work at that cell and tells the owner, with the last reason: a blocker on the cell that the owner holds. Once the owner lets the work go on, the cell runs again. A round the engine cut off itself, a run that ended without a return, and a round that started before the owner last let the work go on are not counted.

failed.desc: A run of the agent's command line that ends without handing in a return is not a return sent back, and is never counted with returns sent back: nothing was wrong with what the agent did, since it never ran to the end. The engine tells the kinds below apart by what the command line reports. None of them asks the owner for a written answer.

kinds.name: usage_limit
kinds.when: The account's usage limit is reached; the command line says when it resets
kinds.desc: The engine starts no new round for any work until the time the command line gives, tells the owner once, then carries on each work from the cell it recorded. One cause stops every work alike, so no work is retried or paused for it on its own.

kinds.name: offline
kinds.desc: The engine starts no new round for any work until the network is back, looking every half minute, tells the owner once if it lasts, then carries on each work from the cell it recorded.

kinds.name: transient
kinds.when: The service is overloaded, returns a server error or times out, or the command line crashes
kinds.desc: The engine runs the same round again: once after a short wait, then, while it still fails, after waits that grow each time up to five minutes, until it passes, and records each attempt on the work.

kinds.name: cannot_run
kinds.when: The login has expired, or the command line cannot be found
kinds.desc: Only the owner can log in again or install the command line, and one cause stops every work alike: the engine starts no new round for any work, tells the owner once, lets one round try every half minute, and once one runs carries on each work from the cell it recorded. The owner logs in or installs, and writes nothing.

kinds.name: prompt_too_long
kinds.when: The prompt is too long for the model
kinds.desc: Running again cannot help: it is a defect of the engine's to fix. The engine pauses the work and tells the owner; once the owner lets the work go on, the same cell runs again.

kinds.name: unparsed
kinds.when: The command line gave up on the agent's return after its attempts at it: the JSON the agent wrote could not be parsed
kinds.desc: Not a passing failure: the round never runs again from its start. The engine repairs the return within the round. First itself, when the text only lacks brackets that close it at its end: it adds exactly those. Then, for any other fault of the JSON's syntax, by the installation's lowest level, once, in a new session with no tools, which may change only the syntax: its repair is taken only when it parses, passes the cell's checks and keeps every other character of the text as it was, and never of a text cut off, one shorter than the command line reported it or that does not end in a closing brace. Then by the agent itself: its session is resumed and told that its JSON could not be parsed and that a quote or a newline inside a text must be escaped, and it hands its return in again. What is repaired or handed in again is taken as any return, and sent back when it does not fit. When none gives a return, the engine pauses the work and tells the owner; once the owner lets it go on, the cell runs again.

record: Each round records, besides the message it was given and each conditional input in it, the whole command line it ran with (the arguments, the structured-output schema, the session it started or resumed), the engine's version and the command line's version, so that what the agent saw can be told afterwards without guessing.

A round whose return the command line could not parse keeps the whole text of each of its attempts, rebuilt from the stream, and how it was repaired or handed in again, with what that cost, which the round's cost includes.
environment: The engine starts every agent's command line with a configuration directory of its own, so the owner's own settings, memory, plugins and tool servers never reach an agent: what an agent is given comes only from the flow and the project's configuration.

Every agent's command line streams each tool input whole, not in pieces, so that the service checks its JSON; tries a return three times, not five, since each attempt writes the whole return again; and gives the stream's partial messages, from which each attempt at a return is rebuilt whole.

engine.name: cut_off
engine.when: The engine stopped, or the work was paused, while the round ran
engine.desc: The round is closed as cut off, and the same cell runs again in the same session, told to look at the worktree as it is and go on.

engine.name: cannot_step
engine.when: A step cannot be taken: the configuration is wrong, or the item is above the highest level
engine.desc: The engine pauses the work with the reason and tells the owner; once the owner lets it go on, the step is taken again.

engine.name: repeats
engine.when: The message would give its session whole what the session already holds
engine.desc: It is not sent: a fault of the engine's. The engine pauses the work and tells the owner; once the owner lets it go on, the cell runs again.

engine.name: work_ended
engine.when: The work ended while its round ran, as when its item was cancelled
engine.desc: What the round hands in is not taken; what it cost is kept on it.
